# {box}-{carrier} modules

So now, after the last 4 chapters talking about the declaration of imports (and the way they are used and reload) whether they are R packages or scripts/folders from the local directory, writing modules in any depth and how they are being reused, and the way to measure the robustness of the module with unit testing using `{testthat}`. Do you ever wonder if those modules can be distributed across different machines while other matters like the resolution of the package dependencies being used and installation of those modules are done at the same time? With `{carrier}`, yes, it is possible — they are called `{box}`-`{carrier}` modules, and it requires few requirements to make it possible. 

This chapter talks about making `{box}` modules you composed into similar to the traditional R packages, where the reusable R codes composed with `{box}` R package can be *packaged*, be distributed, and be simply reusable across different machines. It is recommended to read Chapters 2 and 3 first before diving under this Chapter, since it involves writing and composing modules. 

---

## Rationale

Here's a problem you've run into already if you followed along since Chapter 3: the `module/` we just written only exists on your local machine, and you have to call its path to attach the module. From the [official documentation](https://klmr.me/box/articles/box.html#attaching-modules) talking about global modules, it teaches you on how modules are globally by setting `options(box.path = <place-the-path>)`. This book, however, teaches you the alternative way to make `{box}` modules distributable, installable, and accessible across different machines — introducing `{carrier}`. Most of the steps, such as the resolution of the package dependencies being used on `{box}` modules, are done automatically with `{carrier}` once you run them on terminal. 

## Introducing {carrier}

`{carrier}` is a new tool for R, written in Rust, that makes the distribution and the installation (with resolution) of `{box}` modules possible. When using `{carrier}`, all you need to have is your terminal and any editor you prefer to use to write `{box}` modules. There's no official name for this packages yet, since it is another variation and a new way to write packages in R involving `{box}` module, and that's why they are called `{box}`-`{carrier}` modules. Under the project containing the source code of the module, the root directory must contain one metadata file called `carrier.toml`. This book won't explain everything about the `{carrier}` installation details, the CLI commands,and won't fully explain the metadata itself, instead it is recommended to read the official documentations, under the following links:

-  [Installation Guide](https://joshuamarie.com/carrier/installation.html)
-  [Metadata](https://joshuamarie.com/carrier/reference/carrier-toml.html)
-  [CLI Commands](https://joshuamarie.com/carrier/reference/cli.html)

## Why not just write an R package

Well, there's the traditional CRAN-style R packages already, as long as there's `DESCRIPTION`, `NAMESPACE`, and the built-in `{tools}` package. An existing real R package system already solves the distribution, and there's already decades of support for this system, so why built another approach? 

The thing is that writing a real package around something you were only ever `box::use()`-ing internally costs you more than it gives back. A few things get in the way:

-  Traditional packages spread their metadata across more than one file. `DESCRIPTION` holds the dependency list and package information. Then, we have `NAMESPACE` that holds what gets exported, and neither writes itself, `NAMESPACE` especially usually comes out of an `{Roxygen2}` build step you rerun every time an export changes. A `{box}`-`{carrier}` package holds all of that in the single `carrier.toml` you just saw above, and you'll worry less about the exports since `{box}` already borrows `#' @export` tag. 

-  As explained on this [part](https://modules-in-r.joshuamarie.com/Chapter%203/2-struct-module-1.html#the-structure) from Chapter 1, traditional R packages flatten everything: every written source code are placed under 1 folder `R/`, the declared exports are flatten into 1 namespace, and the module with deep nesting doesn't survive that. If you wish to make everything flat under the module, you just need to pre-export everything through `box::use(./mod[...])` (read this [part](https://modules-in-r.joshuamarie.com/Chapter%202/2-imports.html#wildcard-import) for more details). 

When you actually want is a package produced through modular programming using `{box}`, that's what the rest of this chapter is talking about, along with the `{carrier}` docs linked above, walks through.
